few-samples.t: Suppose the coin truly has **p = 0.8**, but we do not know it. After the first 5 flips, the fraction of heads (the **sample mean**) is a rough, jumpy guess.

running-average.t: After every new flip we recompute the fraction of heads so far. This is the **running average**: each point is the average of **all flips up to that point**.

fluctuation.t: At the start a single flip is a big share of the sample, so the average jumps around: **1.0, 0.5, 0.67, 0.5, 0.6** over the first five flips, then 0.67, 0.71, 0.63 …

more-samples.t: Keep flipping. The horizontal axis is the number of flips, drawn on a **log scale**. A second run of the same coin (pink) **wanders along a different path**.

stabilize.t: By **100 flips** both runs sit near the same level and move much less. By **1000 flips** they are both very close to it.

true-mean.h: THEY SETTLE NEAR THE TRUE VALUE
true-mean.t: That level is the true **p = 0.8**, the expected value of one flip. The running average gets close **without ever being guaranteed to hit it exactly**.

lln-idea.h: WHAT THE LAW SAYS (AND DOES NOT)
lln-idea.t: The **law of large numbers**: as n grows, the sample mean settles toward the expected value. It does **not** say every new flip helps: the pink run was exactly 0.8 at n = 10, then drifted to 0.63 by n = 30 before coming back.

ml-connection.t: An average over more data is a **steadier estimate of an expectation**. That is why the average loss on a big dataset is close to the true expected loss, and why more data gives steadier estimates.
